revision-3:0.prompt: Cheat-sheet check: what are the average-case time complexities of `map.get(key)` and `map.set(key, v)` on a JavaScript Map?
options: O(log n) each, because Map is a balanced tree
O(1) each on average, because Map is hash-based
O(n) each, because Map keeps insertion order
O(1) for get and O(log n) for set
revision-3:0.explanation: The spec requires Map operations to be sublinear on average, and V8 implements Map as a hash table, so get/set/has/delete are O(1) on average. Keeping insertion order doesn't make lookups linear; the order is tracked alongside the hash table.

revision-3:0.prompt: Cheat-sheet check: your API rejects a client for exceeding its request quota. Which HTTP status code should it return?
options: 403 Forbidden
409 Conflict
429 Too Many Requests
503 Service Unavailable
revision-3:0.explanation: 429 means the client sent too many requests, ideally with a Retry-After header. 503 means the server itself is overloaded or down, and 403 means the client isn't allowed at all, regardless of rate.

revision-3:0.prompt: Under the ANSI SQL isolation levels, which anomaly does Repeatable Read prevent that Read Committed allows?
options: Dirty reads
Non-repeatable reads
Phantom reads
Lost updates on unrelated tables
revision-3:0.explanation: Read Committed already prevents dirty reads; Repeatable Read additionally guarantees that re-reading a row gives the same value. In the ANSI definitions phantoms are only ruled out at Serializable (PostgreSQL's snapshot-based Repeatable Read happens to prevent them too).

revision-3:0.prompt: Which sequence lists the main Node.js event-loop phases in the order they run?
options: poll → timers → check → close callbacks
timers → check → poll → close callbacks
check → timers → poll → close callbacks
timers → pending callbacks → poll → check → close callbacks
revision-3:0.explanation: Each loop iteration runs timers, pending callbacks, (idle/prepare), poll for I/O, check (setImmediate), then close callbacks. That's why setImmediate scheduled from an I/O callback runs before a 0 ms timer.

revision-3:0.prompt: Cheat-sheet check: what is the time complexity of inserting into, and removing the top of, a binary heap with n elements?
options: O(1) and O(1)
O(log n) and O(log n)
O(1) and O(n)
O(n) and O(log n)
revision-3:0.explanation: Insert sifts up and extract sifts down along the tree height, which is log n. Only peeking at the top is O(1); building a heap from n items at once is O(n).

revision-3:0.prompt: Reviewing your TypeScript cheat sheet: which of these utility-type notes are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Partial<T> makes every property of T optional
Pick<T, K> keeps only the properties K from T
Omit<T, K> removes the properties K from T
Readonly<T> deep-freezes the object at runtime
Record<K, V> validates object keys at runtime
revision-3:0.explanation: Partial, Pick and Omit are compile-time type transformations. Readonly<T> is shallow and compile-time only (use Object.freeze for runtime), and Record adds no runtime checks; types are erased when compiled.

revision-3:0.prompt: Which statements about CAP and PACELC are correct? Select all that apply.
options: During a network partition, a system must favour either consistency or availability
PACELC adds that, even without a partition, there is a latency vs consistency trade-off
A distributed system can be 'CA' and keep both properties during partitions
Eventual consistency means reads are never stale
Many systems let you tune consistency per operation, e.g. quorum reads and writes
revision-3:0.explanation: CAP's choice applies during partitions; PACELC adds the normal-operation latency vs consistency trade-off; quorum settings (e.g. in Cassandra) make it tunable. 'CA' isn't achievable once partitions happen, and eventual consistency explicitly allows stale reads for a while.

revision-3:0.prompt: The night before an interview, skimming your own condensed notes is usually more useful than starting a brand-new hard topic.
options: True
False
revision-3:0.explanation: Light review reinforces what you already know and keeps it accessible, while a new hard topic is unlikely to stick overnight and can raise anxiety by highlighting gaps.

revision-3:0.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a plain B-tree index on `email` is enough to speed up `WHERE lower(email) = 'a@b.com'`.
options: True
False
revision-3:0.explanation: The index stores email values, not lower(email), so the planner can't use it for that predicate. Create an expression index ON users (lower(email)), or use the citext type.

revision-3:0.prompt: Cheat-sheet check: a POST successfully creates a new order resource. What is the most appropriate response?
options: 200 OK with an empty body
201 Created with a Location header pointing to the new resource
202 Accepted
204 No Content
revision-3:0.explanation: 201 signals that a resource was created, and Location tells the client its URL (often alongside the representation). 202 is for work accepted but not yet completed, such as an async job.

revision-3:0.prompt: A Redis instance used as a cache reaches maxmemory and writes start failing with OOM errors instead of old keys being evicted. What is the most likely cause?
options: Redis can't evict keys without persistence enabled
maxmemory-policy is noeviction (the default); a cache should use allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu
The keys have TTLs, and keys with TTLs can never be evicted
Redis evicts only when a replica is attached
revision-3:0.explanation: With noeviction, Redis refuses writes once it's full. For a cache, allkeys-lru/lfu (or the volatile-* policies when keys have TTLs) lets Redis evict old keys. Persistence and replicas are unrelated to eviction.

revision-3:1.prompt: Why is a full night's sleep before an interview worth more than a few extra hours of study?
options: Sleep helps consolidate memory and restores the attention and working memory problem solving needs
Interviewers can tell visually when you're tired
Studying late is fine as long as you drink coffee in the morning
Sleep only matters for physical tasks
revision-3:1.explanation: Sleep supports memory consolidation, and sleep loss impairs attention and working memory, which are exactly what live coding and design rounds demand. Caffeine can mask sleepiness but doesn't restore the lost cognitive performance.

revision-3:1.prompt: It's 11 pm, your interview is at 10 am, and you still feel shaky on graphs. What's the best plan?
options: Stay up and solve as many graph problems as possible
Skip sleep and review graphs in the morning instead
Switch to learning a completely new topic
Do a short review of your graph cheat sheet, then sleep
revision-3:1.explanation: A brief skim of key patterns keeps them fresh without costing sleep. Late-night cramming trades a small knowledge gain for a large drop in the reasoning and focus you need tomorrow.

revision-3:1.prompt: Which preparation the day before a remote interview prevents the most avoidable problems?
options: Reinstalling your operating system
Buying a new laptop
Testing camera, mic, internet, and the interview tool or editor, and preparing a quiet space
Rewriting your resume
revision-3:1.explanation: Technical hiccups waste interview time and add stress; a dry run of the call link and editor (e.g. CoderPad) plus a charger and quiet room removes most risks. Major system changes the day before create new risks.

revision-3:1.prompt: Mid-interview, your mind goes blank on a problem. What is the best recovery?
options: Say you need a moment, restate the problem, work a small example out loud and start from a brute force
Stay silent until an idea comes
Ask to skip to a different problem immediately
Start writing code at random to look busy
revision-3:1.explanation: Restating and working a concrete example often restarts your thinking and shows a methodical process, and a brute force gives a foothold to optimise. Long silence or aimless coding gives the interviewer nothing to assess or help with.

revision-3:1.prompt: Which habits on the day before an interview usually help performance? Select all that apply.
options: A walk or light exercise
Preparing a few thoughtful questions to ask the interviewer
Planning the schedule, with buffer time before the interview
Drinking strong coffee late at night to study longer
Cramming 20 new hard problems
revision-3:1.explanation: Light activity, prepared questions and a buffered schedule reduce stress and help you show up focused. Late caffeine disrupts sleep, and cramming new problems adds fatigue and anxiety without much retention.

revision-3:1.prompt: Between back-to-back onsite rounds, which actions help you do your best in the next one? Select all that apply.
options: Take a short reset: water, a few slow breaths
Mentally close the previous round instead of replaying it
Glance at your one-page notes for the next round's type
Replay every mistake from the last round in detail
Ask the next interviewer how you did in the previous round
revision-3:1.explanation: A quick physical reset, letting go of the last round and a light refresh help you start fresh. Ruminating drains focus, and the next interviewer typically hasn't seen (and shouldn't share) other rounds' feedback.

revision-3:1.prompt: Pulling an all-nighter before a problem-solving interview usually improves performance, because the material is fresh.
options: True
False
revision-3:1.explanation: Sleep deprivation impairs attention, working memory and flexible thinking, which outweighs any benefit of last-minute review. Recently crammed material is also poorly consolidated without sleep.

revision-3:1.prompt: Some nervousness before an interview is normal, and slow, deliberate breathing is a commonly recommended way to calm it.
options: True
False
revision-3:1.explanation: Moderate arousal is normal and can even sharpen focus; slow breathing (longer exhales) is a widely used, simple way to reduce acute stress before or during a round.

revision-3:1.prompt: You have three onsite loops scheduled in one week. How should you arrange them, if you can?
options: All on the same day to get them over with
With recovery time between the big loops, ideally a lighter day in between
Back-to-back late at night after work
Schedule them without checking any other commitments
revision-3:1.explanation: Full loops are mentally draining; spacing them lets you rest and briefly review between companies. Stacking them causes fatigue that drags down later loops.

revision-3:1.prompt: Which morning-of routine best sets you up for a 10 am interview?
options: Skip breakfast and solve two hard new problems
Eat a normal meal, skim your one-page notes and STAR stories, and join or arrive 10 minutes early
Start a new system design topic to stay sharp
Stay in bed until 9:55 to maximise rest
revision-3:1.explanation: A normal meal, a light refresh of familiar material and a buffer for logistics keep you calm and focused. New hard problems in the morning risk shaking your confidence right before the round.

revision-3:1.prompt: You feel the first round of an onsite went badly. What's the best mindset for the next round?
options: Assume the loop is lost and coast
Tell the next interviewer the first round went badly
Ask to end the loop early
Reset and give the next round full effort; rounds are often scored independently and your sense of how it went is often wrong
revision-3:1.explanation: Interviewers usually write separate feedback, and decisions weigh the whole loop; candidates also often misjudge their own rounds. Coasting or announcing a bad round turns one weak signal into several.
